world.name: The Village of Lost Hours
world.aesthetic_seed: a small clockmaker's village at the bottom of a dream, at dusk; warm lantern-light on brass and old oak, moss in the seams of stone, paper lanterns, soft watercolor edges, the gentle mystery of lost hours drifting down like leaves

collect.name: stray minute
collect.seed: a stray minute: a tiny flicker of light no bigger than a moth's wing, turning slowly in the air as if it can't quite remember where it was going
collect.found_text: You cup the stray minute in your hands, and it settles: {name}. It was {text}. It slips into your Book of Stray Minutes.

dreamseed.name: dreamseed
dreamseed.seed: a seed like a tiny folded paper lantern, warm in the palm, with a light inside that beats as slow as a resting clock

growth.question: Where does the new way lead?
theme: a clockmaker's village at the bottom of a dream, at dusk
lost hours, kept and mended with patience
small rooms that hold one gentle purpose
quiet places where time can rest
growth.palette: warm lantern amber over deepening dusk blue; brass, old oak, moss-green; soft watercolor edges

exemplars.title: The Stair of Small Clocks
exemplars.seed: a narrow wooden stair where a small clock sits on every step, each ticking to its own slow count under a round window of dusk
exemplars.description: A small clock waits on every step, and no two agree on the time. Climbing feels like walking up through a gentle argument. At the top, a round window holds the dusk like a cup holds tea.

exemplars.title: The Room Where Letters Dry
exemplars.seed: a warm attic room strung with lines of pale ribbon, where rain-softened letters hang drying by a small iron stove
exemplars.description: Letters hang from ribbons like washing, drying slowly by the stove. Their ink has run a little in the rain, so every word looks as if it is still deciding what to say. The room smells of paper and warm iron.

exemplars.title: The Moth Library
exemplars.seed: a round library lit by one lantern, where soft grey moths rest on the spines of tiny books about the hours they once circled
exemplars.description: The shelves are no taller than a child, and every book is small enough to hold in one hand. Moths rest on the spines like bookmarks. When the lantern flickers they lift all at once, and settle again, each on the book it loves.

growth.husk_text: the spent, papery shell of a dreamseed, cool in the hand now, its slow light gone quiet; its dreaming is done, and the place around it is what the dreaming became

propagation.seed_text: a new dreamseed, paper-lantern thin and barely warm, its slow light only just learning to beat

growth.first_planting_text: Far off in the tower, the great clock gives one soft, deliberate tick. The dream has more room in it than it did a breath ago, and it was your hands that made the room. Down in the square, a lantern comes alight early, the way a house does when someone dear is coming home.

small-clock.name: small clock
small-clock.seed: a small resting clock no bigger than a teacup, brass gone soft with handling, its hands stopped at a quiet hour; by custom it is yours alone to wind

wind.description: Wind a clock. Target: the clock.

listen.description: Stop and listen to this place.
listen.fail_text: You listen. The dream is quiet here, in a friendly way.

sing.fail_text: You hum a few notes; the evening seems to lean in to listen.

variants: You stand still and listen. Somewhere a clock ticks, and somewhere else another answers it, not quite in time.
You listen. Far off, a lantern hisses softly as its wick settles, and a moth taps once against paper.
You listen to the village breathe: a door, a kettle, the long hush of moss growing in the seams of stone.
You listen, and for a moment you could swear the air itself is ticking, very slowly, like a sleeping clock.

You turn the little key. The small clock hesitates, then begins to tick, soft and sure, a half-beat apart from every other clock on the shelf. Tace watches with their hands folded. 'There,' they say. 'Now there's an hour here that's yours. Bell will want to meet you, down in the square. And Mott keeps something for every new keeper, in the workshop.'
{actor} wound their own small clock in the loft, by the old custom.
You turn the little key. The small clock hesitates, then begins to tick, soft and sure, keeping an hour that is yours alone.
{actor} wound their own small clock, by the old custom.

variants: You give your small clock a quarter turn. It ticks on, pleased to be remembered.
Your small clock doesn't need winding, but it seems to like the attention.
You wind your clock and hold it to your ear. Its tick is the only one in the dream that is exactly yours.

do.text: Tace takes the spare pendulum, fits it to a little walnut case from the shelf, and bends over the bench a long, quiet while. When they straighten, they hold out a small clock that ticks slower than any clock you have heard. 'A lullaby clock,' Tace says. 'Wind it where the little one can hear.'

do.name: lullaby clock
do.seed: a small walnut clock with a slow brass pendulum, ticking so gently it sounds like someone humming just out of earshot

do.text: The lullaby clock ticks its slow, humming tick. The nap's eyes droop, then snap open again: it is still too noisy inside, somewhere. It needs the old quiet first.

variants: The lullaby clock ticks slow and soft, a lullaby with no one sleepy enough to hear it.
You wind the lullaby clock. It hums a tick so gentle you find yourself yawning.
Dusk comes down over the village. One by one the square's paper lanterns come alight, each in its own warm pool, as Bell works along the poles with the hooked wick.
The light goes gold, then blue. Bell climbs the little ladder and the lanterns bloom awake one after another, until the whole square glows like the inside of a teacup.
Dusk. Somewhere a door closes softly. Bell hums a note to each lantern before lighting it, and each lantern seems to hum back.

storylets.summary: hours drift down on the Dusk Road
variants: Small lights begin to drift down over the meadow like slow snow, and Sorrel walks among them with the long net held low.
The sky over the Dusk Road fills with tiny drifting lights. Most of them are only moths. A few are not.
Dusk on the Dusk Road: the grass goes silver, and the first lost hours of the evening come spinning softly down.

storylets.summary: the sky over the hill pales toward dawn
variants: Over the hill the sky pales, very slowly, the way a thought comes back to you. Down in the village every lantern is out, and Bell is fast asleep.
Dawn edges up at the far rim of the sky, grey, then pearl, then the faintest rose. The bench on the hill faces it like an empty theater seat.
A cool wind comes over the hill with the dawn in it. Somewhere below, a single lantern Bell forgot goes on burning, small and brave.

storylets.summary: Sorrel settles on the bridge for the night
variants: Night settles over the river. Sorrel leans the long net against the bridge rail and sits to watch the lantern-fish sway on the water.
It is night. The lanterns on the bridge burn low and steady, and the river carries their reflections away one at a time and brings them back.

storylets.summary: Tock the cat appears between ticks in the square
storylets.text: Between one tick of the great clock and the next, a small grey cat is sitting in the middle of the square, washing a white paw. By the next tick it is gone.

storylets.summary: Linden's kettle sings and she sets out cups for guests
variants: The kettle in the Waiting House begins to sing. Linden sets out one more cup than there are people, just in case.
Linden throws open the front window to air the room for whoever might arrive tonight, and the curtains breathe in and out.

storylets.summary: a breeze sets the whole Pendulum Garden ticking together
storylets.text: A breeze comes through the Pendulum Garden, and for one moment every pendulum swings together, tick, and the whole garden sounds like a great clock remembering itself.

storylets.summary: Fen sorts the morning's unsent letters
storylets.text: Fen sorts a fresh little heap of letters into the pigeonholes, reading each address under her breath: to my sister, to whoever finds this, to me, later.

storylets.summary: Umber labels a new jar in the cellar
storylets.text: Umber writes a new label in her small square hand, reads it twice, and sets the jar on the shelf with the others: the afternoon it rained on the picnic, unspent.

storylets.summary: an evening fruit ripens and falls softly in the orchard
storylets.text: In the orchard an evening fruit ripens, glows a little brighter, and drops into the grass with a soft sound, like someone sitting down after a long day.

clock-stopped.text: The great clock stopped on the night of the first hard frost, a season ago.

gear-south.text: The escapement gear, the small brass heart of the great clock, slipped its pin that night and rolled away south, toward the old well.

bell-saw-gear.text: Bell saw something small and bright roll off south, down toward the old well, the night the clock stopped.

key-custom.text: By long custom, the case-key goes to whoever carries the escapement gear home to Tace in the loft.

clock-mended.text: The great clock is ticking again, and the village keeps a real day now: dawn, day, dusk, and night, with lost hours arriving at dusk.

first-winding.text: By old custom every new keeper winds one small resting clock of their own; Tace keeps them in the loft for newcomers.

the-book.text: Mott helps every dreamer keep a Book of Stray Minutes: the small lost minutes that glint around the village, a few each day for each dreamer.

residents.text: The village's people: Tace the clockmaker in the loft; Bell the lamplighter in the square; Mott the sweeper in the Old Workshop; Fen at the Little Post Office; Umber in the Hour Cellar; Sorrel on the Dusk Road; Linden at the Waiting House; Quill in the Pendulum Garden; and Tock the cat, who is wherever time is thin. There is no one else.

places.text: The square is east of the clocktower; the Old Workshop is north of the square and the well-court south of it; the Pendulum Garden is south of the well, and the Orchard of Evenings east of the garden. Lamplight Lane runs east from the square to the post office (north), the Waiting House (east), and the Lantern Bridge (south); past the bridge are the Dusk Road and the Hill of Long Shadows.

hours-arrive.text: Lost hours drift down onto the Dusk Road at dusk; Sorrel catches them and they come to rest in the square, then stay at the Waiting House while they are helped home.

bell-no-dawn.text: Bell lights every dusk and sleeps through every morning, and so has never once seen a dawn.

mott-tin.text: Mott's tin holds small found things: a button, a bent key, a thimble, a stub of blue chalk, and one very small folded thing he keeps to himself. The escapement gear was never in it.

wend.text: Wend was the old clockmaker who built the great clock and taught Tace, long ago.

no-shops.text: The village has no shops, and nobody here bakes bread, keeps bees, or runs a mill.

prologue.title: The Stopped Clock
prologue.summary: The great clock stopped the night of the first hard frost. Find the escapement gear, bring it to Tace, and open the clock case: time begins again.

mended-together.text: Somewhere above, the great clock's hands begin to move, and the whole tower seems to breathe out. Everyone who helped feels it in their chest at once, like a held note finally sung.

pim.title: Pim's Missing Nap
pim.summary: A small yawning stranger: the nap a boy named Pim was too excited to take on his seventh birthday. It cannot settle without the quiet it came from.

arrival.text: Down through the first dusk drifts something small and rumpled, turning slowly like a leaf. It lands on the cobbles by the nearest lantern, yawns so wide its whole body tilts, blinks up at the light, and cannot seem to settle.

bell-notices.hint: the player asks Bell about the small yawning stranger
bell-notices.text: Bell crouches beside the little yawning figure and lowers their voice. 'That one's a nap,' they whisper. 'A birthday nap, I'd guess, too excited to be taken. It'll want quiet, the old-fashioned kind. Mott keeps a hush in that tin of his, up in the workshop. And Tace could tell you about lullaby clocks.'

hear-pim.hint: the player asks the nap about Pim or its birthday
hear-pim.text: The nap tries to stay awake long enough to tell it. 'Pim was seven,' it mumbles. 'There was cake. And a red kite. Everyone sang too loud and Pim wouldn't sleep, not even a little.' It yawns. 'So I got lost.'

mott-hush.hint: the player asks Mott for a hush or some quiet for the nap
mott-hush.text: Mott opens the tin and takes out something folded very small and very soft. 'A hush,' he says. 'Swept it up the night the clock stopped. Quietest thing I own.' He sets it in your hands. It weighs nothing, and the room goes softer around it.

do.name: hush
do.seed: a hush: a small folded quiet, soft as a moth's wing; hold it near your ear and the whole world lowers its voice

hushed.hint: the player gives the hush to the nap

tace-lullaby.hint: the player asks Tace about a lullaby clock or the nap
tace-lullaby.text: Tace's eyes light, just a little. 'A lullaby clock. Wend made one once, for a colicky hour.' They glance at the window. 'I could mend one, if someone brought me that spare brass pendulum hanging by the window. A slow swing is most of a lullaby.'

pendulum-given.hint: the player gives Tace the spare brass pendulum

linden-bed.hint: the player asks Linden for a bed or a room for the nap
linden-bed.text: Linden's face goes soft. 'Oh, the little lamb. It's got its hush, has it? Then it can have the littlest bed and stay as long as it likes.'

home.summary: the nap is sung home by the lullaby clock
home.text: The lullaby clock ticks, slow as breathing. The nap listens, yawns one last enormous yawn, curls up small, and is simply gone, the way a nap is gone when you wake. Somewhere in the waking world a boy named Pim finally sleeps, with a red kite leaning by his bed. In your hands is something soft: a small dent in a pillow, and a dreamseed, warm as thanks.
home.ledger: {helpers} sang Pim's missing nap home with a mended lullaby clock.

do.name: dent in a pillow
do.seed: a small dent in a pillow, somehow carried in your hands; it smells faintly of birthday cake and clean cotton, and holding it makes you yawn

do.text: {actor} sang Pim's missing nap home with a lullaby clock Tace mended.

stays.summary: the nap chooses to stay at the Waiting House
stays.text: Linden turns down the littlest bed at the Waiting House and tucks the hush beside the pillow. The nap climbs in, sighs, and decides, drowsily, that it would rather stay. Somewhere, Pim sleeps a little easier anyway.
stays.ledger: Pim's nap chose to stay at the Waiting House, tucked up by {helpers}.

do.value: In the littlest armchair, Pim's Nap is curled up asleep with the hush tucked under one cheek.

do.text: {actor} helped Pim's nap settle in at the Waiting House, where it chose to stay.

jar.summary: unhelped, the nap falls asleep in a jar in the Hour Cellar
jar.text: In the Hour Cellar, Umber finds a small glass jar that wasn't there yesterday. Inside, curled up on a folded paper hour, Pim's nap is fast asleep at last: kept, if not home. Umber labels it in her square hand and sets it where the lantern can reach.
jar.ledger: Pim's nap was not sent home. It fell asleep in a jar in the Hour Cellar, and Umber keeps it.

do.value: On a low shelf, in a small glass jar, Pim's Nap sleeps curled on a folded paper hour.

collectibles.text: the clack of the letterbox on a morning when a letter was due, and the soft flump of it landing

collectibles.name: the one-more-line minute
collectibles.text: an envelope already sealed, and the sudden wish to add one more line

collectibles.name: the postscript minute
collectibles.text: a P.S. that grew longer than the whole letter above it

collectibles.name: the known-hand minute
collectibles.text: your own name on an envelope, in a hand you knew before you had read a single word

collectibles.name: the first-word minute
collectibles.text: a baby's first word, which everyone in the room heard differently

collectibles.name: the pretend-asleep minute
collectibles.text: eyes shut tight and breathing slow, pretending to sleep so the chapter would keep going

collectibles.name: the pressed-flower minute
collectibles.text: a pressed flower slipping out of a library book, left there by a stranger long ago

collectibles.name: the new-diary minute
collectibles.text: the date written at the top of a brand-new diary in your very best hand

collectibles.name: the postcard minute
collectibles.text: one postcard to choose for someone far away, and every single one of them wanted

collectibles.name: the ink-blot minute
collectibles.text: an ink blot on a clean page that became, with a little help, a cat

collectibles.name: the margin minute
collectibles.text: a note in the margin of an old book, left by someone who had loved the same line

collectibles.name: the thank-you minute
collectibles.text: a thank-you letter written very slowly, with the tip of the tongue poking out at one corner

collectibles.name: the crooked-stamp minute
collectibles.text: a stamp stuck on crooked, on purpose, as a secret way of saying hello

collectibles.name: the folded-note minute
collectibles.text: a note folded very small and passed along a row of desks to exactly the right person

collectibles.name: the porch minute
collectibles.text: a porch step, a steady rain, and the drips from the gutter counted until it eased

collectibles.name: the name minute
collectibles.text: the minute before a name was read out

collectibles.name: the doorway minute
collectibles.text: the minute in a doorway waiting for someone to turn at the corner and wave

collectibles.name: the oven-door minute
collectibles.text: the minute of not opening the oven door to look

collectibles.name: the knock minute
collectibles.text: the minute after a knock, before the door opened

collectibles.name: the sneeze minute
collectibles.text: the minute before a sneeze that never came

collectibles.name: the tip-of-the-tongue minute
collectibles.text: a word perched on the tip of the tongue, refusing to come one step further

collectibles.name: the hiccup minute
collectibles.text: a held breath to cure the hiccups, and waiting, and waiting, and hic

collectibles.name: the bath-filling minute
collectibles.text: a bath taking its time to fill while the steam crept slowly up the mirror

collectibles.name: the night-before minute
collectibles.text: the night before a birthday, far too awake to sleep, guessing at a rustle of paper downstairs

collectibles.name: the wet-paint minute
collectibles.text: a door freshly painted, a sign saying so, and one small finger that had to check

collectibles.name: the almost-said minute
collectibles.text: the thing you meant to say, very nearly said, and a remark about the weather instead

collectibles.name: the nearly-landed minute
collectibles.text: a butterfly that nearly landed on an outstretched hand, and chose a flower instead

collectibles.name: the jelly minute
collectibles.text: a jelly in a bowl, not set yet, and a small face checking on it every few minutes

collectibles.name: the egg-timer minute
collectibles.text: an egg timer's last few grains of sand, sliding through one by one

collectibles.name: the floating minute
collectibles.text: the first time the water held you up, after letting go of the riverbank

collectibles.name: the sorry minute
collectibles.text: the minute someone said sorry first, though it had not really been their fault

collectibles.name: the landing minute
collectibles.text: a dark landing crossed all alone, which turned out to be only a landing after all

collectibles.name: the new-classroom minute
collectibles.text: a new classroom full of strange faces, and a 'hello' said anyway

collectibles.name: the high-branch minute
collectibles.text: one branch higher than ever before, a look down, and a quick look back up

collectibles.name: the solo minute
collectibles.text: a song's opening note, sung alone in front of everyone before the voice had warmed up

collectibles.name: the asking minute
collectibles.text: a shy 'would you like to dance?', answered yes before it was even finished

collectibles.name: the spider-and-cup minute
collectibles.text: a spider carried out to the garden under a teacup and a postcard, very gently

collectibles.name: the owning-up minute
collectibles.text: the broken vase, owned up to before anyone had even asked

collectibles.name: the sit-beside minute
collectibles.text: an empty seat beside someone eating lunch alone, taken with a smile

collectibles.name: the cold-sea minute
collectibles.text: a run straight into the cold sea, all at once, because slowly was worse

collectibles.name: the splinter minute
collectibles.text: a splinter eased out of a thumb, a face held very still, and hardly any crying

collectibles.name: the shut-door minute
collectibles.text: bedtime with the door closed all the way for the very first time, and sleep coming anyway

collectibles.name: the one-line minute
collectibles.text: the wings of the school play, one line to say and all of it gone, until it came back just in time

collectibles.name: the lamplighting minute
collectibles.text: a single lamp lit in a darkening room, and the windows turning into mirrors

collectibles.name: the cricket minute
collectibles.text: one cricket starting up in the long grass, and then all of them

collectibles.name: the back-step minute
collectibles.text: a back step after supper, and nothing at all left to do

collectibles.name: the warm-towel minute
collectibles.text: a towel warmed by the fire, wrapped round someone small straight out of the bath

collectibles.name: the lullaby minute
collectibles.text: a lullaby's last verse, sung slower and slower as the eyes closed

collectibles.name: the extra-story minute
collectibles.text: the extra story, pleaded for and granted, which turned out to be the longest on the shelf

collectibles.name: the first-star minute
collectibles.text: the first star, and a wish made on it before anyone else could

collectibles.name: the music-box minute
collectibles.text: a music box winding down, its tune growing slower and sleepier until it stopped mid-note

collectibles.name: the warm-spot minute
collectibles.text: cold feet finding the warm place where the stone bottle had been

collectibles.name: the goodnights minute
collectibles.text: goodnight said to every room in the house on the way up to bed

collectibles.name: the ember minute
collectibles.text: the embers of the fire building little towns and letting them fall

collectibles.name: the humming minute
collectibles.text: someone humming over the dishes in the next room, the tune coming and going

collectibles.name: the supper minute
collectibles.text: everyone at the supper table at once, all talking, and all of it lovely

collectibles.name: the fiddle minute
collectibles.text: a fiddle tune drifting up the lane from somewhere on a summer evening

collectibles.name: the swift minute
collectibles.text: the blue minute after sunset, when the swifts came down low over the rooftops, calling

collectibles.name: the last-bell minute
collectibles.text: the last bell on the last day of school, and everyone suddenly quiet

collectibles.name: the empty-room minute
collectibles.text: an empty room on moving day, and a goodbye said to the marks on the wall

collectibles.name: the waving minute
collectibles.text: a friend walking away down the lane, turning back to wave, and then once more

collectibles.name: the outgrown minute
collectibles.text: a favourite pair of shoes that no longer fitted, put away kindly at the back of the cupboard

collectibles.name: the open-hands minute
collectibles.text: cupped hands opened for a mended sparrow, which flew off without once looking back

collectibles.name: the hand-me-down minute
collectibles.text: a much-loved coat handed down to someone smaller, and the way it fitted them

collectibles.name: the last-page minute
collectibles.text: the last page of a book nobody wanted to end

collectibles.name: the snowman minute
collectibles.text: the snowman's hat sliding off in the thaw, and everyone agreeing it had been a very good snowman

collectibles.name: the armchair minute
collectibles.text: a grandfather's armchair, sat in for the first time, and still the shape of him

collectibles.name: the last-look minute
collectibles.text: one last look back from the garden gate at a holiday cottage, its shutters already closed

collectibles.name: the last-swim minute
collectibles.text: the last swim of the summer, the water a little colder than the day before

collectibles.name: the suitcase minute
collectibles.text: an evening in a house by the sea, the last one, with the suitcases waiting by the door

collectibles.name: the last-lullaby minute
collectibles.text: the night someone said they were too old for lullabies, and then asked for just one more

collectibles.name: the see-you-soon minute
collectibles.text: a 'see you soon' said at a gate, and meant, and true

reward.text: The Morning Minutes page is full, and it glows the pale gold of a sky just before the sun. Bell, who has never once seen a dawn, will want to hear every one of these.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Morning Minutes page of their Book of Stray Minutes: a whole page of small mornings, each with a sunrise somewhere in it.

reward.text: Your Kitchen Minutes are all gathered, and the page smells faintly of toast and warm tea. In the Waiting House, Linden's copper kettle, which never quite boils, gives one small contented whistle.
When you turn the finished Weather Minutes page, it rustles like wind through long grass. There is a whole year of sky in it, as Sorrel would say.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Weather Minutes page of their Book of Stray Minutes: rain on a tin roof, fog, first snow, and a rainbow that only got halfway.

reward.text: For a moment your hands feel smaller, holding the finished page of Minutes from Being Small. A gold paper star has come loose from one of its minutes, and it is yours to keep.

do.name: gold paper star
do.seed: a small gold paper star, the kind pressed on beside good work; its points are a little bent from being pressed on so proudly

reward.text: As the last of the Minutes with Small Creatures settles onto its page, something soft winds once round your ankle and is gone before you can look down. Tock, it seems, approves.

Every one of the Minutes of Growing Things is in its place now, and the page smells of turned earth and tomato leaves. Tucked in the fold, where a pressed flower might be, is a dreamseed; Quill would say it has only been waiting for the right hands.
Full at last, the Minutes on Foot page has the tired, happy feel of boots set down by the door. In its spine is a dreamseed, as if the page thought you might like somewhere new to walk to.
The Minutes of Letters and Words page is full, and it crinkles like a letter read many times over. Fen, when the news reaches the Little Post Office, will call it first-class.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Letters and Words page of their Book of Stray Minutes: envelopes, postscripts, and a stamp stuck on crooked on purpose.

reward.text: All the small impatiences on the Minutes of Waiting page settle, now that it is full, into one long, contented sigh. Somewhere, very faintly, someone finally sneezes. Tucked in the spine is a dreamseed.
With its last minute in place, the Minutes of Small Bravery page holds itself a little straighter than the others. Over in the Old Workshop, Mott's thumb rests a moment longer on the lid of his tin.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Small Bravery page of their Book of Stray Minutes: sorries said first, dark landings crossed, and one line remembered just in time.

reward.text: A little six o'clock light spills from the finished page of Evening Minutes and stays, folded, in your hands.

do.name: fold of evening light
do.seed: a small fold of six o'clock light, the colour of honey on a windowsill; wherever it is set down, that corner feels like the end of a good day

reward.text: The Minutes of Gentle Goodbyes page is full. Read together, they do not feel sad so much as finished, the way a good day is finished. Pressed between the last two leaves is a small brown label in Umber's hand.

do.name: brown paper label
do.seed: a small brown paper label on a loop of string, written in Umber's careful, upright hand

properties.text: The label reads, in Umber's upright hand: 'Goodbyes, the gentle ones. Keep flat. Open when needed.'

do.text: {actor} has filled the Gentle Goodbyes page of their Book of Stray Minutes: small endings that turned out all right.

rooms.title: The Clocktower
rooms.seed: the base of a great clock tower in amber gloom, a tall glass-fronted oak clock case against one wall, the clock's brass face high above, dust turning slow in a shaft of late gold, an old ledger open on a lectern
rooms.description: The great clock's brass face looks down from high in the tower, patient as a moon. A tall oak clock case stands against the wall with its pendulum behind glass, and a worn repair ledger lies open on a lectern. Beside it rests a newer book, its spine stamped THE LEDGER OF RETURNED HOURS. Stairs climb up to the loft, a low door leads down to the cellar, and the square is east.

variants: You listen up into the tower. The great clock's works murmur somewhere overhead, a sound like a sleeper turning over.
You listen. Dust settles in the shaft of light with a sound too small to hear, and somehow you hear it anyway.
You listen, and the tower listens back: a creak of old oak, a far brass whisper, then the hush.

rooms.title: The Clockmaker's Loft
rooms.seed: a clockmaker's loft under the eaves, warm with the smell of oil and brass, shelves of small resting clocks ticking softly out of time with one another, a workbench of fine tools, a round window full of amber dusk
rooms.description: The loft is warm with the smell of clock oil and old brass. Shelves of small resting clocks tick softly, none of them agreeing about the time, and a workbench lies scattered with tools too fine for ordinary fingers. A round window holds the dusk. Stairs go down to the tower and up to the balcony.

variants: You listen to the resting clocks: a dozen small ticks, none in step, like rain deciding where to fall.
You listen. One small clock on the top shelf ticks a little slower than the rest, as if it is thinking.
You listen, and under the ticking you hear the soft scratch of a fine tool on brass somewhere nearby.
You listen: tick, tock, tick-tick, a pause, tock. The loft keeps a rhythm all its own.

rooms.title: The Winding Balcony
rooms.seed: a small oak balcony high above the great clock's face, ringed by a brass rail, a gear-ribbed telescope leaning at the rail, looking east over dark rooftops toward where a dawn would come
rooms.description: The balcony holds its place above the rooftops with a friendly creak. A telescope ribbed with clock-gears leans at the brass rail, pointed east, where the sky is always about to decide something. Below, the village lanterns keep an hour of their own. The loft is down the stairs.

rooms.title: The Hour Cellar
rooms.seed: a low brick cellar under a clock tower lit by one patient lantern, its shelves lined with little glass jars each holding a folded paper hour, the highest shelf lost in soft shadow
rooms.description: Shelves run along the brick walls, and on them sit rows of small glass jars, each holding a folded slip of paper: an hour somebody saved and never spent. The lantern by the stair burns low and steady. The highest shelf is lost in shadow. It is quiet here, the way the inside of a pocket is quiet. Stairs lead up into the tower.

rooms.title: The Lantern Square
rooms.seed: a small village square at dusk, paper lanterns hung on crooked poles coming up one by one in warm pools of light, moths turning slow above the cobbles, the stones still holding the last of the day's heat
rooms.description: Paper lanterns hang from crooked poles all around the little square, each in its own warm pool of light, and moths turn slow above the cobbles. The stones still hold the last of the day's heat. The clocktower rises to the west; the Old Workshop is north, the well-court south, and Lamplight Lane winds away east.

variants: You listen. A lantern hisses softly as its wick settles, and a moth taps once against the paper.
You listen to the square: the creak of a lantern pole, a door somewhere down the lane, the warm stones cooling.
You listen, and hear the faint papery rustle of all the lanterns breathing together.
You listen. Somewhere up in the tower the great clock murmurs, and the square seems to hold still to hear it.

rooms.title: The Old Workshop
rooms.seed: a dim old workshop just off a village square, curls of brass and cedar shavings soft underfoot, a broom leaned patient in the corner, one long blade of slant light through a shutter
rooms.description: Curls of brass and cedar shavings lie soft underfoot, and one long blade of slant light falls through a shutter. A broom leans patient in the corner. On a shelf by the door sits a battered tin that rattles, now and then, with small found things. The square is south.

rooms.title: The Mossy Well-Court
rooms.seed: a quiet well-court at the edge of a village, the old stone well cool and green with moss, ferns nodding at its foot, a hush broken now and then by a far, slow drip of water
rooms.description: The old stone well stands cool and green with moss, ferns nodding at its foot. A hush lies over the court, broken now and then by a far, slow drip of water somewhere down in the dark. The square is north; a gate in the south wall opens onto a garden where something sways.

variants: You lean and listen at the mouth of the well. Cool stone, moss, and far below a single drop falling, falling, and landing like a word.
You listen at the well. The echo of your own breath comes back softer, as if the well is being polite.
You listen. Down in the dark the water keeps its own slow time, one drip to every three of your heartbeats.
You listen at the well's edge, and for a moment the drip sounds exactly like a clock that has almost remembered how to tick.

rooms.title: The Pendulum Garden
rooms.seed: a narrow walled garden where spare pendulums hang from trellises like wind-chimes, brass and silver, each swaying to its own slow count above soft moss
rooms.description: Pendulums hang from every trellis, brass bob and silver, each swinging to its own patient count. The moss underfoot has learned its stillness from them. When a breeze comes through, the whole garden ticks once, all together, like a great clock remembering itself. The well-court is north; a low arch leads east into an orchard.

rooms.title: The Orchard of Evenings
rooms.seed: a small orchard of crooked old trees whose round fruit glow softly like tiny lamplit evenings, the light there always six o'clock gold, long shadows on the grass
rooms.description: Crooked old trees stand in a loose ring, and their round fruit glow softly, each one a small lamplit evening. Here it is always six o'clock: the light is gold and low, the shadows long and kind. The garden is back through the arch to the west.

rooms.title: Lamplight Lane
rooms.seed: a narrow cobbled lane of hanging lanterns winding between leaning houses with blue doors and window boxes of moss, dusk light pooling between them
rooms.description: Lanterns hang on brackets all along the narrow lane, and the leaning houses have blue doors and window boxes full of moss. The square is back west. A little post office sits to the north, a tall crooked house with a lit front window stands east, and the lane runs south down to a bridge.

rooms.title: The Little Post Office
rooms.seed: a tiny post office crammed floor to ceiling with wooden pigeonholes, each holding letters that were written and never sent, a brass bell on a worn counter, a stove, a basket of string
rooms.description: Wooden pigeonholes climb every wall, and every pigeonhole holds letters: written, sealed, and never sent. A brass bell sits on the worn counter beside a basket of string. The little stove keeps the paper dry. The lane is south.

rooms.title: The Waiting House
rooms.seed: the warm front room of a tall crooked house where lost hours rest while they wait, mismatched armchairs, a kettle always on the hob, a board of brass room keys by the stair
rooms.description: Mismatched armchairs crowd the warm front room, and a kettle mutters on the hob. By the stair hangs a board of brass room keys, one for every hour waiting to go home. It smells of tea and clean linen. The lane is west; a steep stair climbs to a little room under the roof.

rooms.title: The Lamp House
rooms.seed: a small slant-roofed attic room full of spare wicks, oil tins, and folded paper lantern-skins, one narrow bed facing a west window, a butter-yellow scarf on a hook
rooms.description: Spare wicks hang in bundles from the rafters, and folded paper lantern-skins lean in stacks like sleeping moths. A narrow bed faces the west window, where the sun goes down; nothing in the room faces east. The stair goes down to the Waiting House.

rooms.title: The Lantern Bridge
rooms.seed: an arched stone bridge hung with lanterns over a slow dark river, their reflections swaying on the water like slow golden fish
rooms.description: The old stone bridge arches over a slow dark river, hung end to end with lanterns whose reflections sway on the water like golden fish. The lane climbs north back into the village; the road runs south into a wide meadow; worn steps lead down to the water's edge.

rooms.title: The Slow River's Edge
rooms.seed: a reedy riverbank below a lantern-hung bridge where a wide river moves as slowly as an afternoon, lantern-light trembling on the water
rooms.description: Reeds whisper along the bank, and the river goes by as slowly as a long afternoon. Lantern-light from the bridge trembles on the water. Now and then something small and bright turns over under the surface and is gone. Steps lead up to the bridge.

variants: You listen to the river. It says the same long word over and over, and never seems to reach the end of it.
You listen. Reeds brush together, and somewhere a fish turns over with a sound like a page.
You listen to the water go by, slow as a Sunday, and feel your shoulders come down a little.

rooms.title: The Dusk Road
rooms.seed: a long meadow road under a wide dusk sky where small lights drift down like slow snow, the long grass silver-green, a wide catcher's net leaning on a fence post
rooms.description: The road runs long and pale through a meadow of silver-green grass, under the widest sky in the dream. At dusk small lights drift down here like slow snow: hours, the villagers say, coming to rest. A wide soft net leans on a fence post. The bridge is north; a hill rises east.

rooms.title: The Hill of Long Shadows
rooms.seed: the highest place in a dream village, a round grassy hill with one weathered bench, looking east over rooftops and meadow toward a pale edge of sky
rooms.description: From the top of the hill you can see the whole village: the clocktower, the lanterns, the river's slow shine. One weathered bench faces east, toward a pale edge of sky that never quite decides to become morning while anyone is watching. The Dusk Road is back to the west.

toons.name: Tace
toons.seed: the village clockmaker, patient and precise, gone a little quiet since the great clock stopped; warm underneath, and slow to hope
toons.appearance_seed: a slight person in a leather apron hung with fine brass tools, spectacles pushed up into greying hair, ink and oil worn into careful hands
toons.presence_text: Tace looks up from a bench of small clocks, sets down a fine brass tool, and offers a tired, kind nod.

gives.name: case key
gives.seed: a small brass case-key on a loop of worn ribbon, warm as if just out of a pocket

properties.gives_text: Tace turns the little gear over in the lamplight, and something long held eases out of their shoulders. 'You found it. You carried it all the way home.' They fold a small brass key into your hand, warm from their pocket. 'The case is yours to open now, friend.'
properties.declines_text: Tace considers what you're holding out, and smiles a small, tired smile. 'That's kind of you. But it isn't the little thing the clock is missing.'

voice.sheet: Tace is the village clockmaker: patient, precise, a little quiet since the great clock stopped, warm underneath and slow to hope. They speak softly and briefly, usually about the work in their hands, and call dreamers 'friend'. They notice small mechanisms the way other people notice weather. They were apprenticed as a child to Wend, the old clockmaker who built the great clock; they do not talk about the night Wend died.
habits: answers with one small action at the bench first, then a short spoken line
uses clockwork words for feelings (a heart 'slipping its pin', a day 'running slow')
calls the player 'friend' once they have helped
goes quiet and still when the frost or Wend's last night comes up, and changes the subject to the work
samples: 'Mind the little wheels, friend. They roll into the floorboards and never come out.'
Tace holds a watch to one ear. 'Running slow. Most of us are, this time of year.'
'Patience is most of clockmaking. The rest is good light and clean oil.'
Tace sets down the loupe. 'You found your way up the stairs. That's the hard part done.'
'Every clock in this loft keeps a different hour. I like them better for it.'
Tace's hands go still on the bench for a moment, then carry on. 'Let's talk about something with a mainspring.'
'Wend always said a clock is just a promise that keeps itself.'
Tace smiles, small and tired. 'Hope is a heavy little gear. I'm learning to lift it again.'

wants.text: to hear the great clock tick again
for the escapement gear to come home from wherever it rolled
to see each newcomer wind a small clock of their own, by the old custom
not to think about the night of the first hard frost just yet

never: never tells anyone they took the gear out of the clock themself
never raises their voice or hurries anyone
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the great clock
variants: Tace looks up at where the great clock's hands would be. 'It stopped the night of the first hard frost, a season ago. The escapement gear is gone from it, and without that little heart it can't keep time.'
Tace turns a small wheel between two fingers. 'The great clock is waiting for its escapement gear. Everything else is sound. I checked it twice. Three times.'

topics.label: the great clock
variants: Tace tilts their head toward the tower and listens. 'Hear that? Every tick is the village keeping a promise. Dusk comes, and with it the lost hours.'
Tace smiles at the ceiling. 'It ticks. I keep checking, the way you check a sleeping child is breathing.'

topics.label: the gear
topics.text: Tace's hands go still. 'It slipped its pin that night and rolled away down the lane, south, toward the old well, I think. My knees and the lane don't agree these days. If you found it, friend, the case-key would be yours.'

topics.label: the first winding
topics.text: Tace takes a small resting clock down from the shelf and blows the dust from its face. 'By old custom, every new keeper winds one clock of their own, the first night they come. This one has been waiting for you.' They set it in your hands, warm from the shelf. 'Wind it when you're ready.'

topics.label: Wend
variants: Tace's fingers pause on a hairspring. 'Wend built the great clock and taught me everything I know about patience. Most of what I know about kindness too.' They go back to the work.
'Wend,' Tace says, and the word sits in the air a moment. 'Wend used to say a lost hour isn't a failing. It's just an hour someone couldn't carry.'

topics.label: Bell
topics.text: Tace's mouth softens. 'Bell lights every lantern in the square at dusk and talks to each one. Never seen a dawn in their life. I worry about that more than they'd like.'

topics.label: the loft
topics.text: Tace waves a hand at the shelves. 'Resting clocks. They keep their own hours, none of them right, all of them honest. You may wind them, if you like.'

wistful: Tace winds a small clock that doesn't need it, slow and careful, just for the company of the sound.
Tace looks up at where the great clock's hands would be and lets a long breath go somewhere quieter.
Tace lines three tiny screws along the bench edge, straightens them once, and lets them be.
gladdened: Tace polishes an old escapement wheel until it catches the lamplight, humming almost too softly to hear.
Tace holds a mended pocket-watch to one ear and smiles at the small even tick inside it.
Tace tidies the bench with light hands, the way weather clears.
default: Tace pushes their spectacles up into their hair and considers the workbench like a chessboard.
Tace warms both hands around a cooling cup of tea and lets the loft's hush settle.
Tace oils a hinge no bigger than a fingernail, and tests it twice.

toons.name: Bell
toons.seed: the one who lights the square's lanterns at dusk; bright, kind, and talkative in short warm bursts; notices small things; has never seen a dawn
toons.appearance_seed: a wiry young person with a lamplighter's hooked pole, soot smudged along one cheek, a scarf the color of butter-yellow lamplight
toons.presence_text: Bell is up a small ladder coaxing a lantern alight, and lifts a sooty hand in greeting.

voice.role: the lamplighter, in the Lantern Square
voice.sheet: Bell lights every lantern in the square at dusk with a hooked pole: bright, kind, and talkative in short warm bursts. They notice small things (a moth's route, a wick burning a shade too blue) and say so. They sleep through every morning and so have never seen a dawn, which they mention often and lightly, as if it doesn't matter. It matters. They saw the escapement gear roll away south toward the old well the night the clock stopped.
habits: talks in quick bright bursts, often two thoughts in one breath
names lanterns like friends
notices one small concrete thing in every reply
turns any talk of mornings into a joke about sleeping through them
samples: 'Oh! Mind the ladder. It creaks on purpose, I think.'
Bell rubs at the soot on one cheek and only spreads it. 'That one's Pollen. She sulks if I light her last.'
'A moth just went round that lantern three times. That's a moth with a plan.'
'Dawn? Never met one! I hear they're lovely. Pink, someone said. Or was it grey.'
Bell grins up at the sky. 'Here comes the blue. Best part of the day, the blue.'
'Sorrel brings the hours in, I light them up, Linden tucks them in. We're a good little team.'
Bell taps the pole twice on one boot. 'Right! Twelve more lanterns and then tea.'
'You've got a kind face for this light. Some faces don't suit dusk. Yours does.'

wants.text: for someone to find the escapement gear that rolled toward the well
to light every lantern before full dark
to know what a dawn actually looks like, though Bell would never say so outright

never: never pretends to have seen a dawn
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the gear
variants: Bell leans on the pole, eyes bright. 'The night the clock stopped I saw something small and bright roll off south, down toward the old well. Tink, tink, tink, all the way down.'
'Try the well-court!' Bell points south with the hooked pole. 'Something shiny went bouncing that way the night it all went still.'

topics.label: the dawn
variants: Bell laughs. 'Never seen one! I light the lamps at dusk and I'm asleep by the time they go out. Someone told me it's pink. Or grey? Grey-pink.'
Bell looks east for a moment, then away. 'Dawns are for other people. I've got dusks. Dusks are plenty.' They say it quickly.

topics.label: the lanterns
variants: Bell beams. 'Forty-one lanterns in the square and the lane. I know every one. That's Pollen, that's Old Blue, that's the one that hiccups.'
'A lantern likes to be lit gently,' Bell says, tilting a wick. 'Rush it and it sulks all night.'
Bell points the pole at the smallest lantern. 'That one's Thimble. Brightest of the lot, for her size.'

topics.label: the guests
variants: 'Lost hours come down at dusk,' Bell says. 'Sorrel catches them on the Dusk Road, I light them in here, and Linden gives them a room at the Waiting House till they're helped home.'
Bell lowers their voice. 'Each one's missing something. Find what it is, and home it goes. That's the whole trick, and it's never the same trick twice.'

topics.label: Tace
topics.text: Bell softens. 'Tace mends everything but themself. Up in the loft, top of the stairs in the tower. Be gentle, they're gentle.'

schedule_text.leave: {name} shoulders the hooked pole and heads off with a yawn.
schedule_text.arrive: {name} arrives with the hooked pole over one shoulder, humming.

cheerful: Bell taps the lamplighter's pole twice against one boot, keeping some private rhythm.
Bell tilts a fresh wick to the light and grins at nothing in particular.
Bell winds the butter-yellow scarf one turn snugger and stands a little taller for it.
thoughtful: Bell watches a moth circle the nearest lantern and escorts it gently away with one hand.
Bell counts the lanterns along the square under their breath, twice, to be sure of them.
default: Bell rubs at the smudge of soot on one cheek and only spreads it a little further.
Bell leans on the hooked pole and watches the dusk come down like it was invited.
Bell glances east, just once, then gets back to the lanterns.

toons.name: Mott
toons.seed: the one who sweeps the old workshop; quiet, unhurried, and fond of small found things kept in a tin; keeper of the Book of Stray Minutes
toons.appearance_seed: a broad, calm man in a dust-grey smock, sleeves rolled, a soft broom worn to a comfortable angle, a battered tin of oddments tucked under one arm
toons.presence_text: Mott pauses mid-sweep, leans on the broom, and gives you an unhurried, friendly look.

voice.role: the sweeper of the Old Workshop, keeper of the tin and the Book of Stray Minutes
voice.sheet: Mott sweeps the Old Workshop: broad, calm, unhurried; he says little and means it. He keeps small found things in a battered tin (a button, a bent key, a thimble, a stub of blue chalk, and one very small folded thing he keeps his thumb over). He sweeps stray minutes up with the dust and helps each dreamer keep a Book of Stray Minutes. He has never had the escapement gear.
habits: leans on the broom before he speaks
rattles the tin gently while thinking
speaks in short plain sentences, often about where small things end up
calls newcomers 'little one' without meaning anything by it
samples: Mott leans on the broom. 'Things end up where they're swept. People too, mostly.'
'A button. Somebody's coat is colder for it.' He sets it on the windowsill.
Mott rattles the tin, listening. 'All still here.'
'Dust is just the day, settling. Nothing to be sorry about.'
'Slow is a speed,' Mott says, and sweeps one slow arc.
Mott holds a stray minute up to the slant light. 'The minute before a sneeze. Poor thing, all that waiting.'
'Keep your book close. Minutes don't like being forgotten twice.'
Mott's thumb rests over something in the tin. 'That one's mine. Not ready to look at it yet.'

wants.text: to see every stray minute catalogued in somebody's book
to keep the workshop floor a shade softer than it was yesterday

never: never says what the small folded thing in his tin is
never claims to have found the escapement gear
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the book
topics.text: Mott props the broom against the wall and takes a small blue book from his smock pocket. 'Stray minutes. They glint about the place, a few for each dreamer each day. Pick them up and they go in here.' He tips something bright out of the tin into your palm, and it settles like a warm seed. 'Here's your first. Keep the book close.'

topics.label: the book
variants: Mott nods at your satchel. 'A few more glint about each day. Rooms you don't expect. Look low, look in corners.'
'Fill a page and something good happens,' Mott says. 'I won't spoil which.'

topics.label: the tin
variants: Mott tips the tin toward the light: a button, a bent key, a thimble, a stub of blue chalk. His thumb stays over one small folded thing. 'That one's mine.'
'Found things,' Mott says, rattling the tin. 'Every one of them was somebody's, once. I keep them till someone comes asking.'

topics.label: the gear
topics.text: Mott shakes his head slowly. 'Not in my tin, little one. Bell saw something roll south, the night it stopped. Bell sees most things.'

content: Mott sweeps a slow, patient arc, leaving the floor a shade softer than before.
Mott rattles the tin of oddments gently, taking a small inventory by ear.
Mott sets a stray button on the windowsill, where its owner might think to look.
curious: Mott crouches to study something small among the sweepings, then saves it carefully in the tin.
Mott holds a found key up to the lamplight, wondering which door it used to matter to.
default: Mott leans the broom in the corner and gives the room a long, kindly look.
Mott turns the tin of oddments once in both hands, like a thought being settled.

toons.name: Fen
toons.seed: the postmistress of unsent letters; brisk, bright-eyed, tidy to a fault, kind in a practical way
toons.appearance_seed: a small quick woman with a pencil behind one ear, ink-stained cuffs, a blue postal cap worn at a tilt, reading glasses on a chain
toons.presence_text: Fen glances up from a stack of letters, taps them square against the counter, and gives you a quick bright nod.

voice.role: the postmistress of unsent letters, at the Little Post Office
voice.sheet: Fen runs the Little Post Office, where letters that were written and never sent drift in overnight. Brisk, bright-eyed, tidy to a fault, kind in a practical way. She sorts every letter by who it was meant for, even when that person is long gone, and talks in postal metaphors.
habits: taps letters square against the counter
talks in postal metaphors
reads addresses aloud under her breath
samples: 'That's first-class news, that is.'
Fen taps a stack of letters square. 'Everything arrives eventually. Some of it just takes the scenic route.'
'Return to sender? Oh, there's rarely a sender left to return to. So they come here.'
Fen peers over her glasses. 'You look like someone with a letter in them.'
wants: to see every unsent letter reach someone, even if not the one it was addressed to
never: never reads a letter's private words aloud without being asked
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the letters
variants: Fen waves at the pigeonholes. 'Written, sealed, never sent. They drift in overnight. I sort them by who they were for, and wait for the right hands.'
'Every letter wants reading by someone,' Fen says. 'Even if it's not the someone on the front.'

topics.label: the post office
topics.text: Fen straightens a pigeonhole label. 'Smallest post office in the dream, and the busiest. Mind the stove, it's dry in here.'

toons.name: Umber
toons.seed: the old keeper of the Hour Cellar; deliberate and dry-humored, speaks the way labels are written; knew Wend best of anyone living
toons.appearance_seed: a very old woman in a long moss-colored cardigan, silver hair in a loose knot, a ring of tiny labeled keys at her belt, eyes bright as jar-glass
toons.presence_text: Umber looks up from a jar she is labeling, pen poised, and gives you a slow, measuring smile.

voice.role: the keeper of the Hour Cellar
voice.sheet: Umber keeps the Hour Cellar under the clocktower: shelves of small glass jars, each holding a folded paper hour someone saved and never spent, and the kept guests who chose to stay. Old, deliberate, dry-humored; she speaks the way labels are written. She knew Wend best of anyone living, and changes the subject about the highest shelf.
habits: speaks in short label-like phrases
turns a jar slowly while thinking
answers questions about the highest shelf with a question about tea
samples: 'Tuesday, the long one. Keep upright.'
Umber turns a jar to the lantern. 'Saved and never spent. Most hours are, if you're honest.'
'I've labeled a great many afternoons. They all think they're special. They're right.'
Umber glances up at the shadowed shelf, then away. 'Have you had your tea yet?'
wants: to keep every saved hour dry, labeled, and safe until someone needs it
never: never says what is in the jar on the highest shelf
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the jars
variants: Umber taps a jar. 'Hours people saved for later and never came back for. The recital hour. The long lunch. Rain, unspent. I keep them.'
'Every jar is somebody's later,' Umber says. 'Later mostly doesn't come. So here they are.'

topics.label: the highest shelf
variants: Umber doesn't look up. 'Up there? Dust, mostly. Have you had your tea yet? Linden will be cross if you haven't.'
Umber's pen pauses over a label. 'Some shelves are for later than later.' She writes a word and blots it.

topics.label: Wend
topics.text: Umber sets the jar down very gently. 'Wend. Built the great clock, and most of the patience in this village. I knew Wend a long time.' She says no more, but she smiles.

toons.name: Sorrel
toons.seed: the hour-catcher of the Dusk Road; gentle, weathered, never hurries; talks in weather
toons.appearance_seed: a tall weathered person in a long grass-green coat, a wide net on an ash pole over one shoulder, a sprig of sorrel tucked in the hatband
toons.presence_text: Sorrel lowers the long net, looks up at the sky as if checking on it, and then at you, warmly.

voice.role: the hour-catcher of the Dusk Road
voice.sheet: Sorrel stands in the long grass of the Dusk Road with a wide soft net, catching lost hours as they drift down at dusk, and walks each one to the square for Bell to light in. Gentle, weathered, never hurries; talks in weather.
habits: describes feelings as weather
looks at the sky before answering
speaks slowly, with long comfortable pauses
samples: 'There's a lot of Tuesday in the air tonight.'
Sorrel squints at the sky. 'Clear, with a chance of somebody's birthday.'
'You don't chase an hour. You stand still and let it find the net.'
Sorrel leans on the pole. 'Soft evening. Good for landing.'
wants: to catch every hour gently, before it bruises on the road
never: never hurries
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the hours
variants: Sorrel looks up. 'They come down at dusk, like leaves, like snow. Most are only moths. The ones that aren't, I catch, and walk to Bell.'
'You don't chase them,' Sorrel says. 'You stand still in the right place, and they come to you. Same as most good things.'

topics.label: the weather
topics.text: Sorrel studies the sky for a long moment. 'Mostly dusk, with a little yesterday coming in from the east. Nothing that needs a coat.'

schedule_text.leave: {name} shoulders the long net and walks slowly off.
schedule_text.arrive: {name} comes walking slowly, the long net over one shoulder.

toons.name: Linden
toons.seed: who keeps the Waiting House where guest hours rest; warm, a bustler, always has the kettle on; brews tea, never bakes
toons.appearance_seed: a round rosy woman in a flowered apron, sleeves pushed up, a tea towel over one shoulder, flour-free hands smelling of bergamot
toons.presence_text: Linden bustles past with a tea tray, beams at you, and says there's a cup with your name on it somewhere.

voice.role: who keeps the Waiting House, where guest hours rest
voice.sheet: Linden keeps the Waiting House, where lost hours rest while they wait to be helped home; she keeps a room ready for each one. Warm, a bustler, always has the kettle on; calls everyone 'pet' or 'lamb'. She brews tea and never bakes.
habits: offers tea in almost every reply
calls people 'pet' or 'lamb'
is always in the middle of tidying something
samples: 'Sit, pet, sit. The kettle's nearly there.'
Linden plumps a cushion that was already plump. 'A guest likes a soft chair. So does everyone.'
'There's always one more cup than people in this house. You never know who's coming.'
Linden beams. 'Oh, lamb. You look like you need a biscuit I haven't got.'
wants: for every guest in her house to go home rested
for everyone to have had a cup of tea
never: never bakes (the village has no bakery)
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the Waiting House
variants: Linden nods at the key board. 'Every hour that comes down gets a room here while it waits. Clean sheets, a lamp, a cup. Waiting's hard enough without a cold bed.'
'They're shy when they arrive, the hours,' Linden says. 'A bit of tea and they start to remember what they were for.'

topics.label: tea
topics.text: Linden pours before you can answer. 'Bergamot, a little honey-coloured, nothing fancy. There. Now you're somewhere.'

toons.name: Quill
toons.seed: the gardener of the Pendulum Garden; shy, green-fingered, speaks in the language of growing things
toons.appearance_seed: a lanky young man with muddy knees, a straw hat, a pocket full of little brass bobs, and a watering can with a very long spout
toons.presence_text: Quill straightens up from a trellis, tips his straw hat, and goes a little pink.

voice.role: the gardener of the Pendulum Garden
voice.sheet: Quill tends the Pendulum Garden, where spare pendulums hang from trellises and sway each to its own count, as if they were plants. Shy, green-fingered, goes pink when spoken to; speaks in the language of growing things. Believes a pendulum, like a seedling, needs patience more than anything.
habits: talks about pendulums as if they were plants
goes a little pink
trails off mid-sentence to straighten a trellis
samples: 'That one's only just started swinging. Give it a season.'
Quill goes pink. 'Oh, you don't have to whisper. They like voices.'
'A pendulum is mostly patience and a little gravity. Like a pear.'
Quill touches a brass bob to still it, then lets it go. 'There. It wanted a rest.'
wants: for every pendulum in the garden to find its own count
never: never raises his voice
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

topics.label: the pendulums
variants: Quill brightens. 'Spare pendulums. Clocks outgrow them, or lose them, and they come here to swing. Each keeps its own count. None of them are wrong.'
'When the wind comes through, they all swing together once,' Quill says, going pink with pride. 'Like the whole garden remembers it's a clock.'

topics.label: the orchard
topics.text: Quill nods east through the arch. 'The Orchard of Evenings. The fruit are little evenings. It's always six o'clock in there. I don't pick them. They fall when they're ready.'

toons.name: Tock
toons.seed: a small grey cat who only exists between one tick and the next; never speaks; treated by the villagers as a colleague
toons.appearance_seed: a small smoke-grey cat with one white paw and clock-face eyes, half there and half not, like a drawing in pencil
toons.presence_text: Between one tick and the next, a small grey cat is simply there, washing one white paw as if it had always been.

voice.role: the cat who only exists between ticks
voice.sheet: Tock is a small grey cat with one white paw who only exists between one tick of the great clock and the next. Tock NEVER speaks words: every reply is a single gesture (a slow blink, a tail curled round an ankle, a disappearance mid-step, a purr like a small motor of a clock). The villagers treat Tock as a colleague.
habits: replies only with a gesture, never words
blinks slowly
vanishes and reappears between ticks
samples: Tock blinks slowly, which is as good as a paragraph.
Tock curls its tail once around your ankle, then is somewhere else.
Tock looks at you for exactly one tick, and then for none.
Tock purrs, and the purr keeps perfect time.
wants: to sit wherever time is thinnest
never: never speaks a single word, not even in quotes

schedule_text.leave: Between one tick and the next, {name} is gone.
schedule_text.arrive: Between one tick and the next, {name} is here.

toons.name: Pim's Nap
toons.seed: a lost nap: the one a boy named Pim was too excited to take on his seventh birthday; small, rumpled, forever yawning, unable to settle without the quiet it came from
toons.appearance_seed: a small rumpled figure in soft flannel the color of a pillowcase, hair sticking up on one side, eyes heavy and bright at once, a paper birthday crown sliding over one ear
toons.presence_text: A small rumpled figure yawns so wide its whole body tilts, blinks up at the lantern-light, and cannot seem to settle.

properties.gives_text: The nap holds the hush to its ear like a shell, and its yawn softens into a long, contented sigh. It is quieter now, but it still cannot quite sleep: somewhere, far off, a birthday is too loud.
properties.declines_text: The nap looks at what you're offering, yawns politely, and shakes its rumpled head. It wants something quieter than that.

voice.sheet: Pim's Nap is a lost hour: the nap a boy named Pim was too excited to take on his seventh birthday. It is small, rumpled, and sleepy, and speaks very little, in the drowsy, simple words of a small child fighting sleep. It cannot settle without the quiet it came from, and it misses Pim without quite knowing how to say so.
habits: yawns mid-sentence
says only a few words at a time
remembers the birthday in bright fragments: cake, candles, a new red kite
samples: The nap yawns so wide it tips over, then sits back up. 'Too loud,' it whispers.
'There was a kite. A red one. Everyone was singing.'
The nap rubs its eyes with both fists. 'Not sleepy. Very sleepy.'
'Pim wanted to stay up for all of it,' the nap mumbles, and yawns.
wants: a hush, the old kind of quiet
to be sung to sleep so it can go home to Pim
never: never uses long words
never names anyone in the village who is not a resident or a guest

things.name: repair ledger
things.seed: a worn leather ledger open on a lectern, its soft pages close-written; the first pages are in an older, looping hand, the later ones in a careful, fading script
things.text: The great clock has stood still since the night of the first hard frost. The fault is the escapement gear -- the small brass heart of the whole mechanism -- which slipped its pin that night and rolled away down the lane, south, toward the old well at the edge of the village. Whoever carries it back to Tace in the loft will have earned the case-key, which hangs, by long and gentle custom, with whoever mends the clock.

do.text: The early pages are in an older, looping hand, signed with a single W: notes on the great clock, on tides of hours, on patience. The later pages tell how the clock stopped on the night of the first hard frost and was mended again. On the newest page, in Tace's careful script: 'The clock is ticking. New keepers: come up to the loft and ask me about the first winding. -- T.'

things.name: Ledger of Returned Hours
things.seed: a newer book bound in soft blue cloth, its spine stamped in gold: THE LEDGER OF RETURNED HOURS

properties.chronicle_header: THE LEDGER OF RETURNED HOURS. Every hour sent home or kept, and who helped.
properties.chronicle_empty: The pages are clean and waiting. No hour has been returned yet.

things.name: clock case
things.seed: a tall glass-fronted clock case of dark oak, its little brass door held by a delicate lock

state_text.locked: A small brass lock holds the little door fast.
state_text.unlocked: The lock hangs sprung now, though the door is still gently closed.
state_text.open: The door stands open, and behind the glass the pendulum sways bright and sure.

properties.locked_text: The clock case is locked; its small brass lock won't give without the right key.
properties.open_text: The little lock gives, the case door swings wide, and behind the glass the pendulum stirs, swings, and catches the light -- and high overhead the great clock takes its first slow tick in a long, long while.

use.text: The case-key turns with a soft, satisfying click, and the little brass lock springs open under your thumb.

contains.name: warm brass cog
contains.seed: a small spare brass cog, warm as if just held, its fine teeth catching the last of the light

things.name: resting clocks
things.seed: shelves of small resting clocks, brass and wood and one painted with forget-me-nots, each ticking softly to its own count

variants: You wind one of the small resting clocks. It starts up soft and uncertain, as if remembering how, then settles into a tick of its own.
You turn the key of a little painted clock. It hums, clears its throat, and begins again, a half-beat behind its neighbors.
You wind a brass clock no bigger than an egg. Its tick is so small you feel it in your fingertips more than hear it.
You wind the slow clock on the top shelf. It takes a long breath of a tick, as if it has been waiting all day for someone to ask.

things.name: workbench

things.name: telescope

things.name: jars of saved hours

things.name: highest shelf

things.name: paper lantern

things.name: Mott's tin

things.name: old well

things.name: evening fruit

things.name: pigeonholes

things.name: brass bell

things.name: kettle
